caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No — and the man who made it wanted you to find out.

On October 16, 1869, two men digging a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, hit a stone figure ten feet four and a half inches long, weighing nearly 3,000 pounds. One of them reportedly said, "I declare, some old Indian has been buried here!"

Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes. Three to five hundred people a day came. Cardiff's hotels and restaurants had never been so busy.

It was made of gypsum quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, in 1868 by George Hull, a tobacconist who told the quarrymen the block was for a Lincoln monument. It was carved in Chicago, aged with sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles driven into a board to fake skin pores, then buried on his cousin's farm for a year.

Hull did it after losing an argument at a Methodist revival about the giants in Genesis 6:4. He confessed on December 10, 1869. In court on February 2, 1870, both the giant and P. T. Barnum's plaster copy were declared fakes.

What is not settled: whether the Chicago stonecutter Edward Burkhardt knew what he was making. The record says only that quilts were hung to muffle the sound of the carving.

Images: the giant photographed by Bain News Service, 1910; "The Onondaga Giant" lithograph by Popular Graphic Arts; and an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, from the New York Public Library.

cards.headline: Sold as <y>a petrified man</y>, ten feet long
cards.note: Newell put up a tent and charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing. Three to five hundred people came each day. Printed sheets listed its dimensions: whole length 10 feet 4½ inches.
cards.alt: Lithograph showing a reclining stone figure on a plinth, drawn from the side.

cards.headline: The stone came from <y>an Iowa gypsum quarry</y>
cards.note: In 1868 George Hull hired men at Fort Dodge to cut a block of gypsum ten feet four and a half inches long. He told them it was for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York.

cards.headline: Carved in Chicago, then <y>buried for a year</y>
cards.note: Sculptors worked behind hung quilts to muffle the sound. Hull aged the surface with sand, sulphuric acid, and steel knitting needles set in a board to fake skin pores. Cost: $2,600.
cards.alt: Printed text on the back of an old stereocard describing the Cardiff Giant imposture.

cards.headline: Hull confessed. <y>One question stayed open.</y>
cards.note: He confessed on December 10, 1869. On February 2, 1870, a court declared both his giant and Barnum's plaster copy fakes. Whether the Chicago stonecutter Edward Burkhardt knew what he was making is not clear.
